title: ARIA and Semantic HTML
description: Understand web accessibility principles and ARIA attributes.

options.text: Using ARIA attributes is always better than using semantic HTML elements
options.explanation: The first rule of ARIA is: don't use ARIA if you can use a native HTML element. <button> is better than <div role='button'> — it includes keyboard handling, focus management, and screen reader announcements for free.

options.text: Semantic HTML elements like <nav>, <main>, <article> provide built-in accessibility landmarks
options.explanation: Semantic elements create landmark regions that screen readers use for navigation. <nav> = navigation, <main> = main content, <aside> = complementary. Users can jump between landmarks without reading everything.

options.text: aria-hidden='true' removes an element from the visual display
options.explanation: aria-hidden removes elements from the accessibility tree (screen readers ignore it) but has NO effect on visual display. Use CSS display:none to hide visually. Conversely, visually-hidden CSS class hides visually but keeps in accessibility tree.

options.text: Color alone is sufficient to convey information to all users
options.explanation: WCAG requires that information conveyed by color is also available through other means (text, icons, patterns). ~8% of men have color vision deficiency and cannot distinguish certain color differences.
